source.title: How predictable is language model benchmark performance?

record.tranche_reason: The study back-tests a different measure—benchmark performance predicted from estimated scaled compute—rather than directly testing the original loss-scaling claim. Its results test the downstream-predictability version.
record.gate_note: The study uses the Chinchilla scaling law to map model and dataset sizes to estimated loss or equivalent scaled compute; it does not directly test held-out cross-entropy power laws, their extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. The reported BIG-Bench and MMLU benchmark back-test results bear on V6. Results about other studies cited in the related-work section are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study back-tests how well scale predicts BIG-Bench Hard, MMLU and per-task BIG-Bench performance across 11+ architectures, with loss estimated from N and D via the Chinchilla law. That bears directly on V6. It uses the loss law as a tool and does not measure loss itself, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add two points. First, the authors argue that apparent cross-architecture differences (e.g., PaLM vs GPT-3) are largely explained by scale, chiefly training-data quantity, once the fit uses an S-shaped form. Second, they treat aggregate predictability as support for a scaling-focused view of AI progress, while warning that prediction needs models already above chance.
record.recipe_differences: The study predicts benchmark scores by first mapping model and training-data sizes through a Chinchilla scaling law, then fitting benchmark performance against estimated reducible loss and evaluating with back-tests. It does not reproduce the original held-out-loss scaling measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction error varies with extrapolation distance and starting scale; MMLU predictions are especially error-prone when starting below 2e23 FLOP. The study also reports differences across benchmark tasks and says multiple-choice tasks have higher extrapolation error than exact-string-match tasks at longer distances. Functional-form choice is examined, with sigmoid generally best or joint-best.
record.problems: The authors note that models are evaluated on different task subsets and prompt counts, making comparisons imperfect; model and dataset details are incomplete in places; more recent models may benefit from algorithmic improvements; and training datasets span only a single order of magnitude. Loss is estimated using a scaling-law transformation rather than directly measured on a common test set. Prediction errors are larger for individual tasks and for forecasts from low-performing models.

untested.parts: Loss is never measured; it is estimated from N and D using the Chinchilla law.
No loss extrapolation is tested; back-tests are on benchmark scores only.
No compute-optimal allocation is measured. The Chinchilla D≈20N rule is only used to convert loss to scaled compute.
No controlled shape sweep at fixed parameter count.
Text language models only; no other modalities or training regimes.

Untested: prediction from directly measured loss on a common test set; chain-of-thought or zero-shot prompting; soft metrics such as log-probability; benchmarks beyond BBH, MMLU and BIG-Bench; training sets spanning more than one order of magnitude.
Functional forms are compared for benchmark fits, not for loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits.

missing.what: Comparison with the constant-offset baseline: the sigmoid cuts aggregate prediction error by a factor of two or more versus the chance/offset forecast.
Headline result: BBH MAE of about 6pp when extrapolating across one order of magnitude.
Multiple-choice tasks (116) show sharper growth in extrapolation error than exact-string-match tasks (39) at long distances.
Fitting against estimated training compute instead of Chinchilla-estimated loss gives similar but slightly worse extrapolation. PaLM falls below trend.

Models from different architectures fall on a common trend at similar scaled compute; BBH errors stay below 10pp even around heterogeneous 1e23 FLOP models; MMLU deviates most there (e.g., Yi-6B above trend).
Per-task error by prediction distance and starting scale.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Loss is never measured: it is derived from the Chinchilla law, so V6 is tested as predictability from scale (N, D) rather than from measured pretraining loss. Training sets span only about one order of magnitude. The sources mix fine-tuned and base models. The reader's labels were largely right; movie_recommendation is moved to absent/challenges.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute.
The study back-tests benchmark performance, not predictions of larger-run held-out loss from smaller-run loss fits.
No fixed-compute sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is measured.
Architecture differences are discussed in relation to benchmark performance, but the study does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study examines language-model benchmarks and does not test other modalities or training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The study tests benchmark prediction for BIG-Bench and MMLU with the reported model data and prompting conditions; it does not establish predictability for all downstream tasks or future training regimes.

The study compares functional forms for benchmark-performance back-tests, but does not test whether loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation depend on setup, nor whether loss curves bend away from a single power law.

relationships.condition: Aggregate BBH and MMLU, short horizons (about a doubling of compute), MMLU starting above 2e23 FLOP; well-behaved tasks such as human_organs_senses
relationships.reason: MAE is 3.9pp for BBH (r1) and 4pp for MMLU (r4) across a doubling; human_organs_senses is decently predicted (r10); errors are at least halved versus the offset baseline (text, Section 4.1).
relationships.display_finding: Across a compute doubling, mean absolute error was 3.9 percentage points for BBH and 4 for MMLU, at least halving baseline errors, while human_organs_senses was reasonably predicted.

relationships.condition: Longer prediction distances, starting scales below the point where models beat chance, and individual BIG-Bench tasks
relationships.reason: BBH error rises to 12.5pp at 2 OOM (r2). MMLU error is 10–20pp overall (r3) and 17pp at 1 OOM (r5). Per-task errors are 17–18pp mean and 8.4–8.6pp median, fat-tailed (r6, r9). Errors are larger for high held-out scores (r7, r8). Emergence is only partially predicted on english_proverbs (r11).
relationships.display_finding: BBH error reached 12.5 percentage points across two orders of magnitude, while MMLU errors were 10–20 points overall and 17 points across one order; individual-task errors averaged 17–18 points with medians of 8.4–8.6, increased for high held-out scores, and only partially predicted emergence on the English proverbs task.

statements.correction: BBH MAE: 12.5pp at two orders of magnitude. MMLU MAE: 17pp at one order of magnitude for starting scales above 2e23 FLOP. Cited rows r2,r3,r5,r6: V6 limits_scope.
statements.problem: The numbers and horizon dependence are correct, but the challenges label overstates the evidence from the cited rows: they demonstrate conditional, imperfect predictability rather than its absence or reversal.
